references.authors: Nordestgaard AT, Nordestgaard BG
references.title: Coffee intake, cardiovascular disease and all-cause mortality: observational and Mendelian randomization analyses in 95 000-223 000 individuals
references.n: 95,366 Danes observational; up to 223,414 in genetic analyses
references.finding: Coffee intake showed U-shaped observational associations with CVD and mortality, but genetic variants that raise coffee intake by 42% were not associated with ischaemic heart disease, CVD mortality or all-cause mortality (Mendelian randomization), while an ApoE positive control worked.

references.authors: Nordestgaard AT
references.title: Causal relationship from coffee consumption to diseases and mortality: a review of observational and Mendelian randomization studies including cardiometabolic diseases, cancer, gallstones and other diseases
references.finding: Review of observational and Mendelian randomization studies: lower mortality and cardiometabolic disease with high coffee intake in cohorts (HR 0.85-0.90) is not supported as causal by MR; MR supports only a lower gallstone risk and suggests higher colorectal cancer risk.

references.authors: Kim Y, Je Y, Giovannucci E
references.title: Coffee consumption and all-cause and cause-specific mortality: a meta-analysis by potential modifiers
references.finding: Non-linear inverse association of coffee with mortality, lowest at 3.5 cups/day (RR 0.85); the association persisted in strata by smoking status, age, weight, alcohol and caffeine content.

references.authors: Zhou A, Hyppönen E
references.title: Long-term coffee consumption, caffeine metabolism genetics, and risk of cardiovascular disease: a prospective analysis of up to 347,077 individuals and 8368 cases
references.finding: Coffee-CVD association was non-linear: compared with 1-2 cups/day, CVD odds were 11% higher in non-drinkers, 7% higher in decaf drinkers and 22% higher above 6 cups/day; CYP1A2 caffeine-metabolism genotype did not modify risk.

references.authors: Liu D, Li ZH, Shen D, et al.
references.title: Association of Sugar-Sweetened, Artificially Sweetened, and Unsweetened Coffee Consumption With All-Cause and Cause-Specific Mortality : A Large Prospective Cohort Study
references.finding: Unsweetened and moderately sugar-sweetened coffee were associated with about 16-31% lower mortality versus non-drinkers in a U-shaped pattern, including decaffeinated and instant coffee; a single baseline measure.

references.authors: Marcus GM, Rosenthal DG, Nah G, et al.
references.title: Acute Effects of Coffee Consumption on Health among Ambulatory Adults
references.finding: Randomly assigned coffee days did not significantly raise premature atrial contractions (RR 1.09) but increased premature ventricular contractions (RR 1.51) and daily steps (+1,058) and reduced nightly sleep (-36 min) versus caffeine-avoidance days.

references.authors: Poole R, Kennedy OJ, Roderick P, et al.
references.title: Coffee consumption and health: umbrella review of meta-analyses of multiple health outcomes
references.finding: Umbrella review: coffee was more often associated with benefit than harm, with the largest relative risk reductions at 3-4 cups/day; almost all evidence was observational and graded low quality.

references.authors: Bakuradze T, Lang R, Hofmann T, et al.
references.title: Consumption of a dark roast coffee decreases the level of spontaneous DNA strand breaks: a randomized controlled trial
references.finding: Four weeks of 750 mL/day dark-roast coffee lowered spontaneous DNA strand breaks in blood cells versus water.

references.authors: Cole JB, Florez JC, Hirschhorn JN
references.title: Comprehensive genomic analysis of dietary habits in UK Biobank identifies hundreds of genetic associations
references.finding: GWAS of 85 food-frequency items found 814 loci, many tied to taste, smell and education; MR suggested the top 'healthy' pattern (wholemeal vs white bread) is driven by education-correlated factors and is not strongly causal for coronary disease or diabetes.

references.authors: Inoue-Choi M, Ramirez Y, Cornelis MC, et al.
references.title: Tea Consumption and All-Cause and Cause-Specific Mortality in the UK Biobank : A Prospective Cohort Study
references.finding: Drinking 2 or more cups of (mostly black) tea a day was associated with modestly lower all-cause mortality; observational, single baseline report.

references.authors: Hakim IA, Harris RB, Brown S, et al.
references.title: Effect of increased tea consumption on oxidative DNA damage among smokers: a randomized controlled study
references.finding: Four months of 4 cups/day decaffeinated green tea lowered urinary 8-OHdG in smokers; black tea had no effect.

references.authors: Lagou V, Greyling A, Ferruzzi MG, et al.
references.title: Impact of flavan-3-ols on blood pressure and endothelial function in diverse populations: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
references.finding: Flavan-3-ol interventions (cocoa, tea, apple, grape) lowered office blood pressure (about -2.8 mmHg systolic) and improved flow-mediated dilation.

references.authors: Johnston BC, Zeraatkar D, Han MA, et al.
references.title: Unprocessed Red Meat and Processed Meat Consumption: Dietary Guideline Recommendations From the Nutritional Recommendations (NutriRECS) Consortium
references.finding: NutriRECS panel issued a weak recommendation that adults continue current unprocessed red and processed meat intake, judging the evidence of harm to be of low certainty and the absolute effects small; the article was later corrected.

references.authors: Zeraatkar D, Han MA, Guyatt GH, et al.
references.title: Red and Processed Meat Consumption and Risk for All-Cause Mortality and Cardiometabolic Outcomes: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of Cohort Studies
references.finding: Low-certainty evidence that cutting red or processed meat by 3 servings/week is associated with very small reductions in mortality, cardiovascular disease and type 2 diabetes.

references.authors: Qian F, Riddle MC, Wylie-Rosett J, et al.
references.title: Red and Processed Meats and Health Risks: How Strong Is the Evidence?
references.finding: Critique of NutriRECS: GRADE criteria designed for drug trials are inappropriate for diet; under NutriGRADE the evidence linking red/processed meat to type 2 diabetes is high quality and to mortality moderate; replacement foods matter.

references.authors: Lescinsky H, Afshin A, Ashbaugh C, et al.
references.title: Health effects associated with consumption of unprocessed red meat: a Burden of Proof study
references.finding: Burden of Proof analysis found only weak evidence linking unprocessed red meat with colorectal cancer, breast cancer, type 2 diabetes and ischaemic heart disease, and no evidence for stroke; the lowest-risk intake range spanned 0-200 g/day once heterogeneity was included.

references.authors: Haile D, Harding KL, McLaughlin SA, et al.
references.title: Health effects associated with consumption of processed meat, sugar-sweetened beverages and trans fatty acids: a Burden of Proof study
references.finding: Burden of Proof: processed meat was conservatively associated with at least 11% higher type 2 diabetes and 7% higher colorectal cancer risk, SSBs with at least 8% higher diabetes risk, and trans fat with at least 3% higher IHD risk; all rated two stars (weak or inconsistent evidence).

references.authors: Al-Shaar L, Satija A, Wang DD, et al.
references.title: Red meat intake and risk of coronary heart disease among US men: prospective cohort study
references.finding: Each daily serving of red meat was associated with 11-15% higher CHD risk; substituting nuts, legumes or soy for red meat was associated with 13-17% lower CHD risk.

references.authors: Bouvard V, Loomis D, Guyton KZ, et al.
references.title: Carcinogenicity of consumption of red and processed meat
references.finding: IARC classified processed meat as carcinogenic to humans (Group 1) and red meat as probably carcinogenic (Group 2A), mainly for colorectal cancer; about 18% higher risk per 50 g/day processed meat.

references.authors: Bastide NM, Pierre FH, Corpet DE
references.title: Heme iron from meat and risk of colorectal cancer: a meta-analysis and a review of the mechanisms involved
references.finding: Highest versus lowest haem iron intake was associated with an 18% higher colon cancer risk; reviews lipid peroxidation and N-nitroso mechanisms.

references.authors: Afeiche MC, Gaskins AJ, Williams PL, et al.
references.title: Processed meat intake is unfavorably and fish intake favorably associated with semen quality indicators among men attending a fertility clinic
references.finding: Processed meat intake was associated with fewer morphologically normal sperm and fish intake with higher counts.

references.authors: Afeiche MC, Williams PL, Gaskins AJ, et al.
references.title: Meat intake and reproductive parameters among young men
references.finding: Processed meat intake was inversely associated with total sperm count; unprocessed red meat showed no association.

references.authors: Liu YS, Zhang YX, Wang XB, et al.
references.title: Associations between Meat and Vegetable Intake, Cooking Methods, and Asthenozoospermia: A Hospital-Based Case-Control Study in China
references.finding: Higher unprocessed meat and vegetable intake, and some cooking methods, were associated with lower odds of asthenozoospermia.

references.authors: Ioannidis JPA
references.title: The Challenge of Reforming Nutritional Epidemiologic Research
references.finding: Viewpoint arguing that nutritional epidemiology relies on unreliable self-report, finds implausibly large effects and needs radical reform.

references.authors: Satija A, Yu E, Willett WC, et al.
references.title: Understanding nutritional epidemiology and its role in policy
references.finding: Defends nutritional epidemiology: criticisms often misapply the drug-trial paradigm; diet is a complex, long-term exposure that cohorts with repeated measures and biomarkers can study.

references.authors: Schoenfeld JD, Ioannidis JP
references.title: Is everything we eat associated with cancer? A systematic cookbook review
references.finding: Of 50 random cookbook ingredients, 80% had studies linking them to cancer risk; single studies reported implausibly large effects that shrank to a median RR of 0.96 in meta-analyses.

references.authors: Trepanowski JF, Ioannidis JPA
references.title: Perspective: Limiting Dependence on Nonrandomized Studies and Improving Randomized Trials in Human Nutrition Research: Why and How
references.finding: Argues tiny effect sizes, massive confounding and measurement error make observational nutrition research unreliable and calls for large, long, streamlined randomized trials.

references.authors: Ramsden CE, Hibbeln JR, Majchrzak SF, et al.
references.title: n-6 fatty acid-specific and mixed polyunsaturate dietary interventions have different effects on CHD risk: a meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials
references.finding: Trials that raised linoleic acid specifically (n-6 only) showed a non-significant 13% higher risk of MI or CHD death, versus 22% lower risk in mixed n-3/n-6 trials; trans fat displacement confounded older trials.

references.authors: Ramsden CE, Zamora D, Leelarthaepin B, et al.
references.title: Use of dietary linoleic acid for secondary prevention of coronary heart disease and death: evaluation of recovered data from the Sydney Diet Heart Study and updated meta-analysis
references.finding: Recovered Sydney Diet Heart data: replacing saturated fat with safflower oil (linoleic acid) increased all-cause death (HR 1.62), CVD and CHD death.

references.authors: Ramsden CE, Zamora D, Majchrzak-Hong S, et al.
references.title: Re-evaluation of the traditional diet-heart hypothesis: analysis of recovered data from Minnesota Coronary Experiment (1968-73)
references.finding: Recovered Minnesota Coronary Experiment data: linoleic-acid-rich diet lowered cholesterol 13.8% but gave no mortality benefit, and each 30 mg/dL fall in cholesterol was associated with 22% higher death risk.

references.authors: Hooper L, Al-Khudairy L, Abdelhamid AS, et al.
references.title: Omega-6 fats for the primary and secondary prevention of cardiovascular disease
references.finding: Cochrane: increasing omega-6 fats probably makes little or no difference to all-cause mortality (RR 1.00) or CVD events (RR 0.97); low- to very-low-quality evidence.

references.authors: Hooper L, Martin N, Jimoh OF, et al.
references.title: Reduction in saturated fat intake for cardiovascular disease
references.finding: Cochrane: reducing saturated fat for at least 2 years lowered combined cardiovascular events by about 17%, with benefit greater when replaced by polyunsaturated fat.

references.authors: Li J, Guasch-Ferré M, Li Y, et al.
references.title: Dietary intake and biomarkers of linoleic acid and mortality: systematic review and meta-analysis of prospective cohort studies
references.finding: Highest versus lowest linoleic acid intake was associated with 13% lower total and CVD mortality; each SD of tissue/blood LA with 9-11% lower mortality.

references.authors: Marklund M, Wu JHY, Imamura F, et al.
references.title: Biomarkers of Dietary Omega-6 Fatty Acids and Incident Cardiovascular Disease and Mortality
references.finding: Higher blood linoleic acid was associated with lower total CVD, CVD mortality and ischaemic stroke; arachidonic acid was neutral.

references.authors: Wu JHY, Marklund M, Imamura F, et al.
references.title: Omega-6 fatty acid biomarkers and incident type 2 diabetes: pooled analysis of individual-level data for 39 740 adults from 20 prospective cohort studies
references.finding: Higher linoleic acid biomarkers were associated with 35% lower risk of type 2 diabetes per interquintile range; arachidonic acid was neutral.

references.authors: Borges MC, Haycock PC, Zheng J, et al.
references.title: Role of circulating polyunsaturated fatty acids on cardiovascular diseases risk: analysis using Mendelian randomization and fatty acid genetic association data from over 114,000 UK Biobank participants
references.n: GWAS of 114,999 UK Biobank participants + MR
references.finding: Mendelian randomization did not support a protective effect of genetically higher circulating linoleic acid or omega-3 on cardiovascular disease; estimates for LA were inconsistent and pleiotropy via lipoproteins (FADS locus) is a likely bias.

references.authors: Yuan S, Bäck M, Bruzelius M, et al.
references.title: Plasma Phospholipid Fatty Acids, FADS1 and Risk of 15 Cardiovascular Diseases: A Mendelian Randomisation Study
references.finding: MR: genetically higher plasma linoleic, alpha-linolenic and oleic acid were associated with lower large-artery stroke and venous thromboembolism, but signals were driven by the pleiotropic FADS1 locus.

references.authors: Zhang Y, Sun Y, Yu Q, et al.
references.title: Higher ratio of plasma omega-6/omega-3 fatty acids is associated with greater risk of all-cause, cancer, and cardiovascular mortality: A population-based cohort study in UK Biobank
references.finding: Higher plasma omega-6/omega-3 ratio was associated with higher mortality, but both plasma omega-6 and omega-3 levels were individually associated with lower all-cause, cancer and CVD mortality.

references.authors: Sacks FM, Lichtenstein AH, Wu JHY, et al.
references.title: Dietary Fats and Cardiovascular Disease: A Presidential Advisory From the American Heart Association
references.finding: AHA advisory: replacing saturated fat with polyunsaturated vegetable oil lowers CVD by about 30% in core trials; criticises Sydney (trans-fat margarine) and Minnesota (short, high turnover) trials.

references.authors: Estruch R, Ros E, Salas-Salvadó J, et al.
references.title: Primary Prevention of Cardiovascular Disease with a Mediterranean Diet Supplemented with Extra-Virgin Olive Oil or Nuts
references.finding: Republished PREDIMED: Mediterranean diet with EVOO (HR 0.69) or nuts (HR 0.72) reduced major CVD events versus low-fat advice; results similar after excluding 1,588 participants with protocol deviations.

references.authors: Estruch R, Ros E, Salas-Salvadó J, et al.
references.title: Retraction and Republication: Primary Prevention of Cardiovascular Disease with a Mediterranean Diet. N Engl J Med 2013;368:1279-90
references.finding: NEJM retraction and republication notice for the 2013 PREDIMED report after non-random allocation of household members and at two of 11 sites.

references.authors: Agarwal A, Ioannidis JPA
references.title: PREDIMED trial of Mediterranean diet: retracted, republished, still trusted?
references.finding: BMJ analysis questioning whether the retracted and republished PREDIMED trial should still be trusted as randomized evidence.

references.authors: Delgado-Lista J, Alcala-Diaz JF, Torres-Peña JD, et al.
references.title: Long-term secondary prevention of cardiovascular disease with a Mediterranean diet and a low-fat diet (CORDIOPREV): a randomised controlled trial
references.finding: CORDIOPREV: over 7 years a Mediterranean diet reduced major cardiovascular events versus a low-fat diet (adjusted HR about 0.72-0.75), mainly in men.

references.authors: de Lorgeril M, Salen P, Martin JL, et al.
references.title: Mediterranean diet, traditional risk factors, and the rate of cardiovascular complications after myocardial infarction: final report of the Lyon Diet Heart Study
references.finding: Lyon Diet Heart Study final report: Mediterranean-type diet reduced cardiac death and non-fatal MI (14 vs 44 events) over 46 months.

references.authors: Rees K, Takeda A, Martin N, et al.
references.title: Mediterranean-style diet for the primary and secondary prevention of cardiovascular disease
references.finding: Cochrane: low-quality evidence of little or no effect of PREDIMED on CVD mortality or total mortality but fewer strokes; Lyon trial suggested benefit; two trials excluded for data-reliability concerns; overall uncertainty remains.

references.authors: Singh RB, Dubnov G, Niaz MA, et al.
references.title: Effect of an Indo-Mediterranean diet on progression of coronary artery disease in high risk patients (Indo-Mediterranean Diet Heart Study): a randomised single-blind trial
references.finding: Indo-Mediterranean Diet Heart Study reported large cardiac benefits; PubMed links a 2005 Lancet expression of concern about the data.

references.authors: Guasch-Ferré M, Li Y, Willett WC, et al.
references.title: Consumption of Olive Oil and Risk of Total and Cause-Specific Mortality Among U.S. Adults
references.finding: Olive oil >7 g/day was associated with 19% lower total mortality versus rarely, but not when compared with other vegetable oils combined.

references.authors: Covas MI, Nyyssönen K, Poulsen HE, et al.
references.title: The effect of polyphenols in olive oil on heart disease risk factors: a randomized trial
references.finding: EUROLIVE: olive oils with higher phenolic content raised HDL and lowered oxidized LDL in a dose-dependent way at 25 mL/day.

references.authors: Sarapis K, George ES, Marx W, et al.
references.title: Extra virgin olive oil high in polyphenols improves antioxidant status in adults: a double-blind, randomized, controlled, cross-over study (OLIVAUS)
references.finding: OLIVAUS: high- vs low-polyphenol EVOO for 3 weeks improved antioxidant status, with modest and partly within-arm effects on oxidized LDL.

references.authors: Caruso P, Caputo M, Cirillo P, et al.
references.title: Effects of Mediterranean diet on semen parameters in healthy young adults: a randomized controlled trial
references.finding: Six months of Mediterranean diet versus low-fat diet modestly increased sperm concentration and total count; other parameters unchanged.

references.authors: Ghasemi A, Jaladat AM, Sharifi MH, et al.
references.title: The effects of mediterranean and Persian diet on sexual function and semen parameters quality among infertile men: a randomized controlled trial
references.finding: Two months of a Mediterranean diet improved sperm count, motility and morphology versus control in a single-blind Iranian trial.

references.authors: Agarwal R, Salas-Salvadó J, Davila-Cordova E, et al.
references.title: Mediterranean Diet, Semen Quality, and Medically Assisted Reproductive Outcomes in the Male Population: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
references.finding: Meta-analysis (mostly observational) linking higher Mediterranean-diet adherence to better sperm count and motility; heterogeneity high.

references.authors: Muffone ARMC, de Oliveira Lübke PDP, Rabito EI
references.title: Mediterranean diet and infertility: a systematic review with meta-analysis of cohort studies
references.finding: Meta-analysis of cohorts found the evidence linking Mediterranean diet with fertility outcomes insufficient for clinical recommendations.

references.authors: Karayiannis D, Kontogianni MD, Mendorou C, et al.
references.title: Adherence to the Mediterranean diet and IVF success rate among non-obese women attempting fertility
references.finding: Lowest vs highest Mediterranean-diet adherence associated with lower clinical pregnancy and live birth in women under 35.

references.authors: Barnes LL, Dhana K, Liu X, et al.
references.title: Trial of the MIND Diet for Prevention of Cognitive Decline in Older Persons
references.finding: MIND diet vs control diet with mild calorie restriction for 3 years gave no significant difference in cognition or brain MRI.

references.authors: Wang DD, Li Y, Bhupathiraju SN, et al.
references.title: Fruit and Vegetable Intake and Mortality: Results From 2 Prospective Cohort Studies of US Men and Women and a Meta-Analysis of 26 Cohort Studies
references.finding: Fruit and vegetable intake was associated with lower mortality up to about 5 servings/day (HR 0.87 vs 2 servings), with no further reduction above that; starchy vegetables, juices and potatoes were not associated with benefit.

references.authors: Aune D, Giovannucci E, Boffetta P, et al.
references.title: Fruit and vegetable intake and the risk of cardiovascular disease, total cancer and all-cause mortality-a systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis of prospective studies
references.finding: Fruit and vegetable intake associated with lower CVD and mortality, down to about 800 g/day.

references.authors: Møller P, Vogel U, Pedersen A, et al.
references.title: No effect of 600 grams fruit and vegetables per day on oxidative DNA damage and repair in healthy nonsmokers
references.finding: 600 g/day fruit and vegetables for 24 days did not change oxidative DNA damage or repair.

references.authors: Chiu YH, Gaskins AJ, Williams PL, et al.
references.title: Intake of Fruits and Vegetables with Low-to-Moderate Pesticide Residues Is Positively Associated with Semen-Quality Parameters among Young Healthy Men
references.finding: Low-to-moderate pesticide-residue produce was associated with higher sperm count; total produce intake was not.

references.authors: Kelly SA, Hartley L, Loveman E, et al.
references.title: Whole grain cereals for the primary or secondary prevention of cardiovascular disease
references.finding: Cochrane: no RCT reported cardiovascular events; trials of up to 16 weeks found no difference in total cholesterol and insufficient evidence on blood pressure; low-quality evidence and partial cereal-industry funding.

references.authors: Aune D, Keum N, Giovannucci E, et al.
references.title: Whole grain consumption and risk of cardiovascular disease, cancer, and all cause and cause specific mortality: systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis of prospective studies
references.finding: Each 90 g/day of whole grain was associated with 19% lower CHD and 17% lower all-cause mortality.

references.authors: Reynolds A, Mann J, Cummings J, et al.
references.title: Carbohydrate quality and human health: a series of systematic reviews and meta-analyses
references.finding: Fibre intakes of 25-29 g/day were associated with 15-30% lower mortality and cardiometabolic disease; trials showed lower body weight, blood pressure and cholesterol with higher fibre.

references.authors: Zargarzadeh N, Mousavi SM, Santos HO, et al.
references.title: Legume Consumption and Risk of All-Cause and Cause-Specific Mortality: A Systematic Review and Dose-Response Meta-Analysis of Prospective Studies
references.finding: Higher legume intake was associated with 6% lower all-cause mortality and lower stroke mortality but not CVD, CHD or cancer mortality; low-to-moderate certainty.

references.authors: Reed KE, Camargo J, Hamilton-Reeves J, et al.
references.title: Neither soy nor isoflavone intake affects male reproductive hormones: An expanded and updated meta-analysis of clinical studies
references.finding: Neither soy nor isoflavone intake affected testosterone, free testosterone, estradiol or oestrone in men.

references.authors: Vanegas JC, Afeiche MC, Gaskins AJ, et al.
references.title: Soy food intake and treatment outcomes of women undergoing assisted reproductive technology
references.finding: Higher soy isoflavone intake was associated with higher live birth rates in a fertility-clinic cohort.

references.authors: Seidelmann SB, Claggett B, Cheng S, et al.
references.title: Dietary carbohydrate intake and mortality: a prospective cohort study and meta-analysis
references.finding: U-shaped association of carbohydrate intake with mortality (lowest at 50-55% energy); replacing carbohydrate with animal fat/protein was associated with higher mortality (HR 1.18) and with plant sources lower mortality (HR 0.82).

references.authors: Shan Z, Guo Y, Hu FB, et al.
references.title: Association of Low-Carbohydrate and Low-Fat Diets With Mortality Among US Adults
references.finding: Healthy (plant-based) low-carbohydrate and low-fat diet scores were associated with lower mortality; unhealthy versions with higher mortality.

references.authors: Gardner CD, Trepanowski JF, Del Gobbo LC, et al.
references.title: Effect of Low-Fat vs Low-Carbohydrate Diet on 12-Month Weight Loss in Overweight Adults and the Association With Genotype Pattern or Insulin Secretion: The DIETFITS Randomized Clinical Trial
references.finding: DIETFITS: healthy low-fat and healthy low-carbohydrate diets produced similar 12-month weight loss.

references.authors: Soto-Mota A, Flores-Jurado Y, Norwitz NG, et al.
references.title: Increased low-density lipoprotein cholesterol on a low-carbohydrate diet in adults with normal but not high body weight: A meta-analysis
references.finding: LDL cholesterol rose on low-carbohydrate diets in people with lower BMI and fell in people with high BMI.

references.authors: Hall KD, Guo J, Courville AB, et al.
references.title: Effect of a plant-based, low-fat diet versus an animal-based, ketogenic diet on ad libitum energy intake
references.finding: People ate about 690 kcal/day more on an animal-based ketogenic diet than on a plant-based low-fat diet.

references.authors: Liu D, Huang Y, Huang C, et al.
references.title: Calorie Restriction with or without Time-Restricted Eating in Weight Loss
references.finding: Adding 8-hour time-restricted eating to calorie restriction gave no significant extra weight loss at 12 months.

references.authors: Peters B, Schwarz J, Schuppelius B, et al.
references.title: Intended isocaloric time-restricted eating shifts circadian clocks but does not improve cardiometabolic health in women with overweight
references.finding: Intended isocaloric early or late time-restricted eating shifted circadian clocks but did not improve insulin sensitivity or cardiometabolic markers.

references.authors: Templeman I, Smith HA, Chowdhury E, et al.
references.title: A randomized controlled trial to isolate the effects of fasting and energy restriction on weight loss and metabolic health in lean adults
references.finding: Alternate-day fasting without energy deficit had no metabolic benefit; with a deficit it lost less fat than daily calorie restriction.

references.authors: Allaf M, Elghazaly H, Mohamed OG, et al.
references.title: Intermittent fasting for the prevention of cardiovascular disease
references.finding: Cochrane: intermittent fasting beat no intervention for weight loss but differed little from continuous calorie restriction.

references.authors: Semnani-Azad Z, Khan TA, Chiavaroli L, et al.
references.title: Intermittent fasting strategies and their effects on body weight and other cardiometabolic risk factors: systematic review and network meta-analysis of randomised clinical trials
references.finding: Network meta-analysis: intermittent fasting and continuous restriction gave similar weight and cardiometabolic changes; alternate-day fasting had a small edge.

references.authors: Hamsho M, Shkorfu W, Ranneh Y, et al.
references.title: Is isocaloric intermittent fasting superior to calorie restriction? A systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs
references.finding: Isocaloric intermittent fasting was not superior to calorie restriction overall; some fat-mass and insulin differences, with more hunger and fatigue on IF.

references.authors: Trepanowski JF, Kroeger CM, Barnosky A, et al.
references.title: Effect of Alternate-Day Fasting on Weight Loss, Weight Maintenance, and Cardioprotection Among Metabolically Healthy Obese Adults: A Randomized Clinical Trial
references.finding: Alternate-day fasting produced similar weight loss to daily calorie restriction at 1 year with higher dropout.

references.authors: Chen M, Xu L, Van Horn L, et al.
references.title: Association of eating duration less than 8 h with all-cause, cardiovascular, and cancer mortality
references.finding: Eating duration under 8 h (from two 24-h recalls) was associated with higher CVD mortality (HR 2.35) but not all-cause mortality, which did not survive sensitivity analyses; authors flag residual confounding.

references.authors: Lin S, Cienfuegos S, Ezpeleta M, et al.
references.title: Time-Restricted Eating Without Calorie Counting for Weight Loss in a Racially Diverse Population : A Randomized Controlled Trial
references.finding: 8-hour time-restricted eating without calorie counting gave weight loss similar to calorie counting over 12 months.

references.authors: Manoogian ENC, Wilkinson MJ, O'Neal M, et al.
references.title: Time-Restricted Eating in Adults With Metabolic Syndrome : A Randomized Controlled Trial
references.finding: Adding time-restricted eating to standard care gave only a small HbA1c reduction (-0.10%).

references.authors: Sundfør TM, Svendsen M, Tonstad S
references.title: Effect of intermittent versus continuous energy restriction on weight loss, maintenance and cardiometabolic risk: A randomized 1-year trial
references.finding: Intermittent (2 days/week) and continuous energy restriction gave similar weight loss and cardiometabolic changes at 1 year.

references.authors: Harvie MN, Pegington M, Mattson MP, et al.
references.title: The effects of intermittent or continuous energy restriction on weight loss and metabolic disease risk markers: a randomized trial in young overweight women
references.finding: 5:2-style intermittent restriction gave weight loss similar to continuous restriction at 6 months.

references.authors: Wei M, Brandhorst S, Shelehchi M, et al.
references.title: Fasting-mimicking diet and markers/risk factors for aging, diabetes, cancer, and cardiovascular disease
references.finding: Three monthly 5-day fasting-mimicking cycles lowered weight, blood pressure and IGF-1 versus usual diet.

references.authors: Brandhorst S, Levine ME, Wei M, et al.
references.title: Fasting-mimicking diet causes hepatic and blood markers changes indicating reduced biological age and disease risk
references.finding: Fasting-mimicking cycles were associated with lower estimated biological age in exploratory analyses.

references.authors: Laurens C, Grundler F, Damiot A, et al.
references.title: Is muscle and protein loss relevant in long-term fasting in healthy men? A prospective trial on physiological adaptations
references.finding: A 10-day fast caused weight loss of which much was lean tissue, with recovery after refeeding.

references.authors: Wilhelmi de Toledo F, Grundler F, Bergouignan A, et al.
references.title: Safety, health improvement and well-being during a 4 to 21-day fasting period in an observational study including 1422 subjects
references.finding: Uncontrolled observational data from a fasting clinic reported weight loss and well-being during 4-21-day fasts.

references.authors: Il'yasova D, Fontana L, Bhapkar M, et al.
references.title: Effects of 2 years of caloric restriction on oxidative status assessed by urinary F2-isoprostanes: The CALERIE 2 randomized clinical trial

audit.claim: Paper-filtered coffee at 3-4 cups/day lowers DNA strand breaks and isoprostanes in RCTs, and cohorts show the lowest mortality at 3-4 cups/day.
audit.biases: The mortality curve rests on cohorts, where non-drinkers include people who stopped for health reasons (reverse causation, 'sick quitters') and coffee tracks smoking and socioeconomic status (residual confounding) [adiet-poole2017]. The DNA strand-break trials are small, short and partly industry-linked [adiet-bakuradze2015].
audit.newer_evidence: Kim 2019 found the inverse association held within never-smokers and other strata, which argues against simple smoking confounding [adiet-kim2019]. But Mendelian randomization using caffeine-intake variants found no genetic link with ischaemic heart disease or mortality (2016) [adiet-nordestgaard2016], and a 2022 review of all coffee MR studies found no support for causal protection against mortality, heart disease, stroke, diabetes or obesity, only for gallstones [adiet-nordestgaard2022]. UK Biobank shows a U/J shape, with higher CVD risk above 6 cups/day and in non-drinkers [adiet-zhou2019], and similar U-shaped mortality associations for decaf, instant and lightly sweetened coffee [adiet-liu2022], a pattern consistent with healthy-user effects as well as with non-caffeine compounds. Coffee MR has its own problem: caffeine-metabolism variants change how much people drink but also how fast they clear it, so null MR is not decisive. The 2023 CRAVE randomized n-of-1 trial found no rise in atrial ectopy but more ventricular ectopy and less sleep on coffee days [adiet-marcus2023].
audit.bottom_line: Coffee up to about 3-4 cups a day is safe for most adults and may be mildly beneficial, but the 15-17% lower mortality in cohorts is probably partly confounded and is not confirmed by genetic studies.

site_change.headline: The biggest single polyphenol (chlorogenic acid) source in many Western diets; small RCTs at 3-4 cups/day lowered DNA strand breaks and isoprostanes, and cohorts link 3-4 cups/day with ~15% lower mortality, though Mendelian randomization studies do not confirm that the mortality benefit is causal.
site_change.note: Add the MR evidence and the J-shape (risk rises above ~6 cups/day) to caveats; fill the empty debate field with [adiet-kim2019] vs [adiet-nordestgaard2022].

audit.claim: Black tea showed no oxidative-DNA benefit in a smoker RCT, while UK Biobank links 2+ cups/day with 9-13% lower mortality.
audit.biases: The mortality figure is from a single baseline questionnaire in a health-conscious volunteer cohort (healthy-user bias, residual confounding) [adiet-inouechoi2022]. Diet-intake genetic instruments partly capture education and taste, so tea MR studies are weak [adiet-cole2020].
audit.newer_evidence: No trial has tested black tea on hard outcomes. Pooled RCTs of flavan-3-ol foods show a small blood-pressure effect (about -2.8 mmHg), mostly from cocoa and green tea [adiet-lagou2025]. The only oxidative-damage RCT remains null for black tea [adiet-hakim2003].
audit.bottom_line: Black tea is harmless; its link with lower mortality may be confounded, so 'neutral' is the fair rating.

audit.claim: Four cups/day of green tea cut urinary 8-OHdG by 31% in heavy smokers and flavan-3-ol foods lower blood pressure slightly, but evidence in healthy non-smokers is weak.
audit.biases: The headline trial is in heavy smokers with high baseline damage; generalising to non-smokers risks overstatement [adiet-hakim2003]. Cohort tea associations are prone to healthy-user confounding and genetic instruments for tea are weak [adiet-cole2020].
audit.newer_evidence: A 2025 meta-analysis of 145 RCTs confirms a small blood-pressure and FMD effect of flavan-3-ols [adiet-lagou2025]. The 12-month Minnesota Green Tea Trial showed liver-enzyme rises with high-dose extract, underlining that extracts are a different exposure from brewed tea [adiet-yu2017].
audit.bottom_line: Brewed green tea is safe and has small vascular benefits; claims of broad antioxidant protection in healthy people remain unproven.

audit.claim: IARC classes processed meat as carcinogenic and red meat as probably carcinogenic, with heme-driven lipid peroxidation and N-nitroso formation; evidence rated strong.
audit.biases: Cohort associations come from food-frequency questionnaires and heavy meat eaters differ in smoking, obesity, alcohol and fibre intake (residual confounding, measurement error) [adiet-zeraatkar2019, adiet-ioannidis2018]. IARC classifies how certain a hazard is, not how large it is [adiet-bouvard2015].
audit.newer_evidence: NutriRECS (2019) rated the evidence low certainty and advised people to continue current intake [adiet-johnston2019, adiet-zeraatkar2019]; nutrition epidemiologists replied that GRADE is unsuited to diet and that substitution matters [adiet-qian2020]. Substitution analyses suggest replacing red meat with nuts, legumes or soy is associated with 13-17% lower CHD risk [adiet-alshaar2020]. The independent Burden of Proof analyses found only weak evidence for unprocessed red meat (2022) [adiet-lescinsky2022], and for processed meat a conservative minimum of 11% higher diabetes and 7% higher colorectal cancer risk, rated two stars (2025) [adiet-haile2025]. Mechanistic support (haem iron) is unchanged [adiet-bastide2011].
audit.bottom_line: Processed meat probably raises colorectal cancer and diabetes risk modestly; for unprocessed red meat the case is weak and depends on what replaces it. 'Strong' overstates how certain and how large the effect is.

site_change.headline: IARC classifies processed meat as carcinogenic (Group 1) and red meat as probably carcinogenic (2A); independent 2022-2025 reviews find the processed-meat link consistent but modest (at least ~7% higher colorectal cancer risk) and the unprocessed-red-meat link weak, with heme-driven lipid peroxidation and N-nitroso formation as the likely mechanism.
site_change.note: Fill the empty debate field: NutriRECS [adiet-johnston2019] vs [adiet-qian2020]; add Burden of Proof results [adiet-lescinsky2022, adiet-haile2025].

audit.claim: Processed meat is the meat signal for sperm: high intake is linked to fewer normal-form sperm and lower counts; observational only.
audit.biases: Two small US studies with food-frequency questionnaires; confounding by overall diet, BMI and abstinence time is plausible [adiet-afeiche2014a, adiet-afeiche2014b].
audit.newer_evidence: No randomized or genetic study of meat and semen quality was found. The general-health evidence on processed meat is consistent but modest [adiet-haile2025].
audit.bottom_line: A reasonable, low-cost precaution, correctly labelled limited and observational.

audit.claim: Unprocessed red meat is not linked to worse semen quality.
audit.biases: Absence of association in small observational studies, with recall bias in the case-control study [adiet-afeiche2014b, adiet-liu2022b].
audit.newer_evidence: Nothing newer on semen. For general health, the 2022 Burden of Proof review rated unprocessed red meat's links with disease as weak [adiet-lescinsky2022].
audit.bottom_line: A neutral rating fits: the evidence for harm from unprocessed red meat is weak.

audit.claim: The 'toxic seed oil' claim is not supported; higher linoleic acid intake and blood levels are linked to lower mortality, though omega-6 trials are mixed.
audit.biases: Cohort intake data are confounded by overall diet, but blood/adipose LA biomarkers reduce reliance on questionnaires [adiet-li2020, adiet-marklund2019]. On the other side, the trials suggesting harm are old, small, and in the Sydney case used a trans-fat-containing margarine [adiet-sacks2017].
audit.newer_evidence: Biomarker pooling (FORCE) links higher LA with lower CVD [adiet-marklund2019] and 35% lower type 2 diabetes per interquintile range [adiet-wu2017]; UK Biobank shows lower mortality with higher plasma omega-6 [adiet-zhang2024]. Mendelian randomization is less supportive: the largest MR study (2022) found no protective effect of genetically higher LA on CVD and warns of FADS-locus pleiotropy [adiet-borges2022]; another found benefit only for stroke and VTE, driven by FADS1 [adiet-yuan2019]. Ramsden's 2010 trial meta-analysis showed n-6-specific trials gave no benefit (RR 1.13) while mixed n-3/n-6 trials did [adiet-ramsden2010], consistent with the recovered Sydney and Minnesota data [adiet-ramsden2013, adiet-ramsden2016] and Cochrane's null omega-6 result [adiet-hooper2018]. Cochrane 2020 supports replacing saturated fat [adiet-hooper2020].
audit.bottom_line: Seed oils are not toxic and replacing butter or lard with them is reasonable; whether extra linoleic acid itself prevents heart disease is unproven by trials and genetics.

site_change.note: Add [adiet-ramsden2010] and the Mendelian randomization results [adiet-borges2022] to the debate field; the 'beneficial' direction is fair for replacing saturated fat, not for adding LA on top.

audit.claim: Industrial trans fats raise LDL, lower HDL, promote inflammation and carry the highest coronary risk per gram of any fat.
audit.biases: Much of the original evidence was cohort-based, open to confounding by fast-food diets [adiet-mozaffarian2006b].
audit.newer_evidence: A natural experiment in New York State showed counties that restricted trans fat had a 6.2% extra drop in MI and stroke admissions versus comparable counties (2017) [adiet-brandt2017], a design that sidesteps individual confounding. The 2025 Burden of Proof review rated the dose-response evidence two stars, with at least 3% higher IHD risk across usual intakes [adiet-haile2025].
audit.bottom_line: The harm is about as well established as any diet finding; most countries have now removed most industrial trans fat, so the practical risk is lower than before.

site_change.note: Cite the New York natural experiment [adiet-brandt2017] in caveats or debate.

audit.claim: PREDIMED cut major CVD events by ~30%; sub-studies found less oxidative damage; for sperm and IVF the data are observational.
audit.biases: PREDIMED was retracted and republished in 2018 after non-random allocation of household members and at some sites [adiet-estruch2018r]; critics question whether it can still be treated as a randomized trial [adiet-agarwal2019]. The control group got low-fat advice rather than a true low-fat diet, and free EVOO or nuts. Fertility associations are cohort and cross-sectional (healthy-user bias) [adiet-muffone2023].
audit.newer_evidence: Republished PREDIMED results held after excluding 1,588 irregular participants [adiet-estruch2018]. Cochrane (2019) judged evidence low quality for mortality, found fewer strokes, and excluded two secondary-prevention trials for data-reliability concerns [adiet-rees2019]; separately, the Indo-Mediterranean Diet Heart Study carries a 2005 Lancet expression of concern [adiet-singh2002]. CORDIOPREV (2022), a 7-year RCT in 1,002 coronary patients, found ~25-28% fewer cardiovascular events than with a low-fat diet [adiet-delgadolista2022], adding to the Lyon trial [adiet-delorgeril1999]. For sperm, two small RCTs (2020, 2025) found modest improvements in count [adiet-caruso2020, adiet-ghasemi2025]; for IVF outcomes no RCT exists and a 2023 meta-analysis called the evidence insufficient [adiet-muffone2023].
audit.bottom_line: The Mediterranean diet remains the best-supported dietary pattern for heart disease, with two independent trials besides PREDIMED; effect sizes are uncertain and the fertility claims remain mostly observational.

site_change.note: Add CORDIOPREV [adiet-delgadolista2022] and the Agarwal/Ioannidis critique [adiet-agarwal2019] to the debate field; sperm entry can cite the two small RCTs [adiet-caruso2020, adiet-ghasemi2025].

audit.claim: High-phenolic EVOO lowers oxidized LDL (EUROLIVE), carries an EU health claim, and PREDIMED's EVOO arm cut major CVD events by ~30%; evidence rated strong.
audit.biases: PREDIMED tested a whole Mediterranean diet plus free oil against low-fat advice, so it cannot isolate EVOO, and its randomization problems weaken it [adiet-estruch2018, adiet-agarwal2019]. Olive-oil cohorts are subject to healthy-user and socioeconomic confounding; in US cohorts olive oil was no better than other vegetable oils combined [adiet-guaschferre2022].
audit.newer_evidence: EUROLIVE's surrogate result (oxidized LDL falling with phenol content) still stands [adiet-covas2006]; the 2022 OLIVAUS crossover found smaller, partly within-arm effects [adiet-sarapis2022]. Cochrane rated the PREDIMED-type evidence low quality for mortality [adiet-rees2019]. No trial has compared high- vs low-phenolic oil on clinical events.
audit.bottom_line: EVOO is a good default fat with a real but modest effect on LDL oxidation; the 30% event reduction belongs to the whole PREDIMED diet, not to the oil alone.

site_change.headline: In the 200-man EUROLIVE RCT, oxidized LDL fell with olive-oil phenolic content at 25 mL/day, and the EU authorises an LDL-protection claim at 5 mg hydroxytyrosol per 20 g; PREDIMED's Mediterranean diet with EVOO cut major CVD events by ~30%, but that trial tested the whole diet, not the oil alone.

audit.claim: A handful of nuts a day lowers LDL and apoB, PREDIMED's nut arm cut CVD events by ~28%, and 60-75 g/day nuts improved sperm quality in two RCTs.
audit.biases: PREDIMED caveats apply [adiet-agarwal2019]; nut trials are often nut-industry funded, including FERTINUTS [adiet-salashuetos2018b].
audit.newer_evidence: Lipid lowering is consistent across 26 walnut trials [adiet-guaschferre2018]. A 2024 meta-analysis pooled the two sperm RCTs (223 men) and confirmed better motility, vitality and morphology, but found no link with ART outcomes in observational studies [adiet-cardoso2024, adiet-robbins2012].
audit.bottom_line: Nuts reliably improve blood lipids and probably sperm parameters in healthy men; fertility outcomes are untested.

audit.claim: Cohorts linked MIND adherence to 53% lower Alzheimer risk, but the 3-year MIND RCT was null.
audit.biases: Reverse causation and food-questionnaire error apply; this is a textbook case of a cohort finding not replicated by a trial [adiet-barnes2023].
audit.newer_evidence: The 2023 NEJM MIND trial was null for cognition and MRI [adiet-barnes2023]. Diet MR is weak because food-intake genetics track education [adiet-cole2020].
audit.bottom_line: The cohort association should not be read as causal: the 3-year trial was null.

audit.claim: DASH lowered BP ~8/7 mmHg and blunted lipid-induced F2-isoprostane rise in one small study; evidence rated limited.
audit.biases: The oxidative-stress claim rests on a single 2003 study [adiet-lopes2003]; the blood-pressure effect is randomized and replicated.
audit.newer_evidence: A 2020 meta-analysis of 30 RCTs (5,545 people) found DASH lowered BP by 3.2/2.5 mmHg, moderate-quality evidence [adiet-filippou2020]. The 2025 Cochrane review found too few trials with events to say whether DASH prevents heart attack or stroke [adiet-bensaaud2025].
audit.bottom_line: DASH is a proven blood-pressure diet (moderate evidence), though the average effect is smaller than the 8 mmHg in the cited study and hard-outcome trials are lacking.

site_change.headline: Across 30 RCTs DASH lowers blood pressure by about 3/2.5 mmHg (more with high salt intake and in younger people); one small study also showed less lipid-induced F2-isoprostane rise, and no trial has yet measured heart attacks or strokes.
site_change.note: The -8.1 mmHg figure is from one obese hypertensive group and is about 2.5x the pooled effect.

audit.claim: Doubling produce lowered some oxidative markers but another trial was null; cohorts show lower mortality up to ~800 g/day; low-pesticide produce linked to higher sperm counts.
audit.biases: Produce intake marks wealth, education, non-smoking and exercise (healthy-user, residual confounding); FFQ measurement error is large [adiet-trepanowski2018, adiet-satija2015]. The sperm finding depends on a pesticide-residue classification in one cross-sectional study [adiet-chiu2016].
audit.newer_evidence: The largest dose-response analysis (2021, 1.9 million people) found mortality benefit plateaued at about 5 servings/day (~400 g), with no extra benefit above that and none from starchy vegetables or juice [adiet-wang2021], lower than the ~800 g in the 2017 analysis [adiet-aune2017]. The oxidative-marker trials remain split [adiet-moller2003].
audit.bottom_line: Eating about 5 servings a day is well supported; benefits beyond that are uncertain and some of the cohort association is likely confounding.

site_change.note: Change 'cohorts show lower mortality up to ~800 g/day' to note the 2021 analysis plateau at ~5 servings/day [adiet-wang2021]; dose 'ideally up to ~800 g' should say benefit beyond ~5 servings is uncertain.

audit.claim: Each 90 g/day whole grain is associated with ~19% lower CHD and 17% lower mortality; evidence rated moderate.
audit.biases: Whole-grain eaters are more educated and health-conscious; a UK Biobank genetic analysis suggested the wholemeal-vs-white-bread pattern is driven by education-linked factors and is not strongly causal for heart disease or diabetes [adiet-cole2020].
audit.newer_evidence: Cochrane (2017) found no RCT with cardiovascular outcomes, and trials up to 16 weeks showed no difference in total cholesterol and insufficient evidence on blood pressure, with partial cereal-industry funding [adiet-kelly2017]. The cohort association itself is consistent [adiet-aune2016], and the Lancet carbohydrate-quality reviews found trial support for higher fibre more than for whole grain per se [adiet-reynolds2019].
audit.bottom_line: Whole grains are a sensible choice over refined grains, but the size of the mortality benefit is uncertain and may be partly confounded.

site_change.note: Add [adiet-kelly2017] to caveats: no RCT on events and no clear lipid effect in trials.

audit.claim: 25-29 g/day fibre is linked to 15-30% lower mortality and cardiometabolic disease; most polyphenols need gut bacteria.
audit.biases: Observational mortality data share the healthy-user problem [adiet-satija2015].
audit.newer_evidence: The Lancet series combined cohorts with trials showing that higher fibre lowers weight, blood pressure and cholesterol, giving the association a causal pathway [adiet-reynolds2019].
audit.bottom_line: Well supported; the link from the microbiome to oxidative stress remains the weak part.

audit.claim: Legumes help glycaemic control and fibre intake; direct oxidative data are scarce.
audit.biases: Mortality associations are observational [adiet-zargarzadeh2023].
audit.newer_evidence: A 2023 meta-analysis of 32 cohorts found 6% lower all-cause mortality and lower stroke mortality with higher legume intake, but no association with CVD or cancer mortality; low-to-moderate certainty [adiet-zargarzadeh2023]. Substituting legumes, nuts or soy for red meat was associated with lower CHD [adiet-alshaar2020].
audit.bottom_line: Modest and consistent but small benefits.

audit.claim: Soy does not change male hormones; equol production varies; soy intake linked to higher ART live birth in one cohort.
audit.biases: The ART association is from one fertility-clinic cohort (residual confounding by diet pattern) [adiet-vanegas2015].
audit.newer_evidence: The 2021 meta-analysis of clinical studies remains the best evidence that soy does not lower testosterone [adiet-reed2021]. No newer trial on fertility outcomes was found.
audit.bottom_line: Neutral is the right reading.

audit.claim: Keto is proven for epilepsy and improves HbA1c, triglycerides and CRP short-term; LDL can rise in lean people; animal-based patterns link to higher mortality.
audit.biases: The low-carb mortality data are cohort-based and confounded by what replaces carbohydrate [adiet-seidelmann2018].
audit.newer_evidence: Meta-analysis confirms LDL rises in lower-BMI people [adiet-sotomota2024]; an inpatient trial showed higher energy intake on animal-based keto [adiet-hall2021]. Seidelmann (2018) found a U-shaped carbohydrate-mortality curve, higher mortality when carbohydrate was replaced by animal fat and protein, lower when replaced by plant sources [adiet-seidelmann2018]. The PCOS and testosterone effects track weight loss [adiet-arsenaki2026, adiet-furini2023]. The 2026 KETO-CTA paper was retracted.
audit.bottom_line: Keto works for epilepsy and improves HbA1c and triglycerides short-term; LDL can rise, especially in lean people, and replacing carbohydrate with animal rather than plant fat and protein tracks higher mortality.

site_change.note: Cite [adiet-seidelmann2018] alongside Shan 2020 for the animal-vs-plant mortality contrast.

audit.claim: Moderate low-carb lowers HbA1c, triglycerides and CRP, matches low-fat for weight at 12 months, and plant-based versions are linked to lower mortality.
audit.biases: Mortality data are observational; questionnaire-based diet scores mix food quality with carbohydrate amount [adiet-shan2020].
audit.newer_evidence: DIETFITS showed equal weight loss for healthy low-fat and low-carb [adiet-gardner2018]; the ARIC/meta-analysis U-shape with plant vs animal substitution shows that the source of the replacement fat and protein matters [adiet-seidelmann2018].
audit.bottom_line: Accurate as written.

audit.claim: Intermittent fasting works mainly by reducing calories; it matches calorie restriction and shows no fasting-specific oxidative benefit.
audit.biases: Early positive findings came from uncontrolled or tiny studies; calorie-matched designs remove confounding by energy deficit [adiet-templeman2021].
audit.newer_evidence: A 2025 BMJ network meta-analysis of 99 RCTs [adiet-semnaniazad2025] and a 2025 meta-analysis of 20 isocaloric RCTs [adiet-hamsho2025] found IF not superior to continuous restriction, with more hunger. Calorie-matched TRE (Liu 2022, Peters 2025) added nothing [adiet-liu2022c, adiet-peters2025]; Cochrane agrees [adiet-allaf2021].
audit.bottom_line: Confirmed: fasting schedules are a way to eat less, not a separate antioxidant intervention.

audit.claim: An 8-10 h window cuts intake and gives weight loss similar to calorie counting; it adds little when calories are matched; the NHANES 'HR 2.35' finding is heavily confounded.
audit.biases: The 2024 AHA abstract, published 2025, used two 24-h dietary recalls, the all-cause association did not survive sensitivity analyses, and the authors themselves flag residual confounding; reverse causation (illness, food insecurity, skipped meals) is plausible [adiet-chen2025].
audit.newer_evidence: Randomized trials: TRE plus calorie restriction was no better than calorie restriction (2022) [adiet-liu2022c]; TRE without counting matched counting (2023) [adiet-lin2023]; in metabolic syndrome only -0.10% HbA1c (2024) [adiet-manoogian2024]; isocaloric TRE did not improve cardiometabolic health (2025) [adiet-peters2025].
audit.bottom_line: The newest trials show eating windows work mainly through eating less; the NHANES '91% higher heart death' claim should be discounted.

audit.claim: ADF gives the same 1-year weight loss as daily restriction with more dropouts; calorie-matched ADF did not lower oxidative stress markers.
audit.biases: The early oxidative-stress result came from an uncontrolled 10-person study.
audit.newer_evidence: Trepanowski 2017 and Templeman 2021 stand [adiet-trepanowski2017, adiet-templeman2021]; the 2025 network meta-analysis found only a small ADF edge [adiet-semnaniazad2025].
audit.bottom_line: Accurate.

audit.claim: 5:2 matches continuous restriction for weight loss with more hunger and hypoglycaemia on glucose-lowering drugs.
audit.biases: None beyond small, short trials.
audit.newer_evidence: One-year trials and meta-analyses agree [adiet-harvie2011, adiet-sundfor2018, adiet-semnaniazad2025].
audit.bottom_line: Accurate.

audit.claim: One 100-person trial showed lower weight, BP and IGF-1; the developer has a commercial interest.
audit.biases: Single research group with a commercial product; biological-age result exploratory [adiet-wei2017, adiet-brandhorst2024].
audit.newer_evidence: No independent replication found in this search.
audit.bottom_line: Accurate; the conflict-of-interest caveat is the key point.

audit.claim: Multi-day fasts lowered TBARS in uncontrolled cohorts, but much of the weight lost is lean tissue and no controlled trial shows lasting benefit.
audit.biases: Clinic-run uncontrolled cohorts (selection, no comparator) [adiet-wilhelmidetoledo2019].
audit.newer_evidence: Controlled physiology work confirms large lean-tissue loss [adiet-laurens2021]; no RCT found.
audit.bottom_line: Accurate.

audit.claim: In CALERIE, ~12% calorie restriction for 2 years lowered F2-isoprostanes, LDL, BP, CRP and insulin resistance, with some bone and lean loss.
audit.biases: Randomized; main limits are adherence and generalisability to lean young adults.
audit.newer_evidence: CALERIE secondary analyses confirm isoprostane falls [adiet-ilyasova2018], cardiometabolic gains [adiet-kraus2019] and only a small effect on one epigenetic pace-of-aging measure [adiet-waziry2023].
audit.bottom_line: One of the best-supported claims in the group.

audit.claim: Experimental overfeeding raises isoprostanes and carbonyls within days to weeks.
audit.biases: Small, short experiments; but they are experiments, so confounding is not the issue [adiet-samochabonet2012, adiet-boden2015].
audit.newer_evidence: No contradicting work found.
audit.bottom_line: Accurate.

audit.claim: Late carbohydrate loads worsen glucose tolerance (more in MTNR1B carriers); weight-loss timing trials are mixed; no oxidative data.
audit.biases: Cohort findings on late eaters are confounded by sleep, chronotype and shift work.
audit.newer_evidence: Both sides: the acute crossover trial [adiet-garaulet2022] and front-loading meta-analysis [adiet-young2023] versus a null controlled crossover [adiet-ruddickcollins2022] and isocaloric early vs late TRE [adiet-peters2025].
audit.bottom_line: Accurate and current.

audit.claim: Cocoa flavanols improve FMD and lower BP; in COSMOS 500 mg/day did not significantly reduce total CVD events or cognition overall.
audit.biases: Many vascular trials are short and cocoa-industry funded; COSMOS's CVD-death benefit is a secondary outcome [adiet-sesso2022].
audit.newer_evidence: COSMOS ancillary work (2025) found an 8.4%/year relative fall in hsCRP but no change in IL-6 or TNF-alpha [adiet-li2025]; COSMOS-Clinic cognition was null [adiet-vyas2024]. Vascular benefits remain consistent in pooled RCTs [adiet-hooper2012, adiet-lagou2025].
audit.bottom_line: Strong for vascular function and blood pressure; unproven for heart attacks, strokes or cognition.

site_change.note: Optionally add the 2025 COSMOS hsCRP result [adiet-li2025]; keep 'strong' tied to the vascular endpoints only.

audit.claim: One cup a day improved endothelial function over 6 months; small trials show oxidative-marker and cognitive benefits.
audit.biases: Small trials, often industry-funded, with many outcomes (multiplicity) [adiet-curtis2019].
audit.newer_evidence: A 2026 meta-analysis of 14 RCTs in healthy people confirmed better FMD (+1.11 points) but found no effect on blood pressure, executive function or mood [adiet-he2026].
audit.bottom_line: Vascular benefit holds; the cognitive claims should be presented as unconfirmed.

site_change.note: Caveat 'Cognitive trials are positive but small' should add that a 2026 meta-analysis found no cognitive effect in healthy people [adiet-he2026].

audit.claim: Pooled berry RCTs show small improvements in LDL, BP, glucose and TNF-alpha; anthocyanin foods improve FMD.
audit.biases: Heterogeneous small trials [adiet-huang2016].
audit.newer_evidence: No newer contrary synthesis found; blueberry-specific 2026 data support FMD but not BP [adiet-he2026, adiet-fairliejones2017].
audit.bottom_line: Accurate and appropriately modest.

audit.claim: Polyphenol-rich, but only one feeding trial, on metabolism not oxidative stress.
audit.biases: Inference by analogy.
audit.newer_evidence: Nothing newer found beyond the feeding study [adiet-solverson2018].
audit.bottom_line: Accurate.

audit.claim: A famous 10-patient study was not replicated by an 18-month RCT and lipids are unchanged in meta-analysis.
audit.biases: Industry-funded small early studies.
audit.newer_evidence: Davidson 2009 and a 12-RCT lipid meta-analysis remain the best evidence [adiet-davidson2009, adiet-sahebkar2016].
audit.bottom_line: A small positive study was overturned by a larger trial.

audit.claim: Red wine has negligible resveratrol, resveratrol is poorly bioavailable, and alcohol raises lipid peroxidation; no antioxidant reason to drink.
audit.biases: The old 'French paradox' and J-curve rested on cohorts where 'non-drinkers' include sick former drinkers (abstainer bias) and light drinkers are healthier [adiet-zhao2023].
audit.newer_evidence: A 2023 meta-analysis of 107 cohorts correcting for former-drinker bias found no mortality benefit from low-volume drinking [adiet-zhao2023]. Linear and non-linear Mendelian randomization in UK Biobank found alcohol raised hypertension and coronary risk at all intakes, and that light drinkers' apparent benefit was explained by healthier lifestyles [adiet-biddinger2022]. Resveratrol metabolites did not predict mortality [adiet-semba2014].
audit.bottom_line: Treating red wine as a harm is better supported now than before: the apparent protection was mostly abstainer bias.

site_change.note: Add [adiet-zhao2023] and [adiet-biddinger2022] to debate: the protective J-curve is largely abstainer bias and healthy-drinker confounding.

audit.claim: Fish oil does not raise oxidative markers; long-chain omega-3 slightly reduces CHD; fish eaters have better sperm counts and a DHA RCT lowered SDF; serum omega-3 linked to IVF live birth.
audit.biases: Fish-eater associations are confounded by wealth and overall diet; fish also carries methylmercury, which may blunt cardiovascular benefit [adiet-mozaffarian2006]. Sperm and egg data are small trials and cohorts [adiet-martinezsoto2016, adiet-chiu2018].
audit.newer_evidence: VITAL (2019): 1 g/day omega-3 did not reduce major CVD events [adiet-manson2019]. Supplement trials raise atrial fibrillation risk by 25%, more above 1 g/day [adiet-gencer2021], echoed in UK Biobank fish-oil users without CVD [adiet-chen2024]. Cochrane remains low-certainty for CHD [adiet-abdelhamid2020]. A meta-analysis of small RCTs supports omega-3 for sperm count and motility [adiet-salashuetos2018].
audit.bottom_line: Eating oily fish once or twice a week is reasonable; high-dose supplements bring a small atrial-fibrillation risk and no clear heart benefit in healthy people.

site_change.note: Add the atrial fibrillation signal [adiet-gencer2021] to 'too_much' for supplements above ~1 g/day; the sperm entry's 'above ~3 g/day raises bleeding risk' should also mention AF.

audit.claim: A glucose load transiently raises leukocyte ROS; sugary drinks linked to ~10 points lower motility in young men.
audit.biases: The ROS data are acute mechanistic studies [adiet-mohanty2000]; the semen link is cross-sectional with a single sample [adiet-chiu2014].
audit.newer_evidence: A 2023 umbrella review found many harmful associations, the strongest (moderate quality) for weight gain and ectopic fat [adiet-huang2023]; Burden of Proof rated SSB-diabetes evidence two stars [adiet-haile2025]. For sperm, results conflict: a 2024 preconception cohort found ~22% lower concentration with 7+ SSBs/week [adiet-joseph2024], while 1,047 Danish young men showed no strong association [adiet-meldgaard2022]; SSBs were linked to lower fecundability in both partners [adiet-hatch2018].
audit.bottom_line: Limiting sugary drinks is well supported for general health; the semen effect is plausible but inconsistent.

audit.claim: 30 g/day milled flaxseed lowered systolic BP by ~10 mmHg (15 in hypertensives), one of the largest BP effects of any food.
audit.biases: A single trial in peripheral artery disease patients; large effects in single small trials tend to shrink [adiet-rodriguezleyva2013, adiet-schoenfeld2013].
audit.newer_evidence: A 2023 meta-analysis of 33 trials (2,427 people) found an average -3.2/-2.6 mmHg, with very high heterogeneity; effects were larger at >=30 g/day, >20 weeks and in hypertension [adiet-li2023].
audit.bottom_line: Flaxseed probably lowers blood pressure a little (about 3 mmHg on average); the 10-15 mmHg figure is the best case from one trial.

site_change.headline: 30 g/day milled flaxseed lowered systolic BP by about 10 mmHg in a 110-patient RCT, but across 33 trials the average fall is about 3 mmHg, larger in hypertension and with longer use; lignans and ALA both appear to contribute.

audit.claim: Nitrate-rich greens and beetroot lower systolic BP by ~4 mmHg in short trials.
audit.biases: Short, small trials (7-30 people each in the 2013 meta-analysis) [adiet-siervo2013].
audit.newer_evidence: A 2023 meta-analysis found -2.4 mmHg systolic in healthy people and no significant fall in hypertensive patients, including 24-h ambulatory BP [adiet-zhang2023].
audit.bottom_line: Nitrate's blood-pressure effect is smaller than early trials suggested and may not hold in people with hypertension; greens remain a good food.

site_change.note: Replace the -4.4 mmHg key number with a range noting the 2023 result (-2.4 mmHg in normotensives, null in hypertensives) [adiet-zhang2023].

audit.claim: Sprouts reliably deliver sulforaphane and raised benzene detoxication ~60% in RCTs, but proof of lower oxidative damage or clinical benefit in healthy people is thin.
audit.biases: Small trials, many from a few groups; a pattern of striking small positive trials followed by null replications [adiet-houghton2016].
audit.newer_evidence: The Qidong detoxication trials hold [adiet-egner2014]. Elsewhere sulforaphane's record is mixed: the 2014 autism trial (44 men) [adiet-singh2014] was not replicated on primary outcomes in 2021, 2023 or a 108-child 2024 trial [adiet-zimmerman2021, adiet-magner2023, adiet-ou2024]; 150 umol/day did nothing to Nrf2, inflammation or MDA in haemodialysis [adiet-ribeiro2024]; COPD was null [adiet-wise2016]; a 2025 prediabetes trial of sprout extract missed its primary endpoint [adiet-dwibedi2025].
audit.bottom_line: Sprouts are a sound way to get sulforaphane, but clinical benefits are unproven and several replications have failed.

site_change.note: Fill the empty debate field with the failed-replication series [adiet-singh2014] vs [adiet-zimmerman2021, adiet-magner2023, adiet-ou2024] and [adiet-ribeiro2024].

audit.claim: Seed powder with active myrosinase converts 30-40% to sulforaphane but outcome trials are scarce.
audit.biases: Pharmacokinetic studies only; products vary.
audit.newer_evidence: Concentrated sulforaphane trials at 150 umol/day failed to change Nrf2 or oxidative markers in haemodialysis [adiet-ribeiro2024] and a broccoli sprout extract trial in prediabetes missed its primary endpoint, with benefit confined to exploratory responder subgroups [adiet-dwibedi2025].
audit.bottom_line: Accurate; outcome benefit is unproven.

audit.claim: Raw broccoli gives far more sulforaphane than cooked; high-glucoraphanin broccoli lowered LDL 5-7% in two RCTs.
audit.biases: LDL trials by one group using a commercial variety [adiet-armah2015].
audit.newer_evidence: No contradicting trials found; crucifer mortality associations remain weak-to-suggestive in umbrella review [adiet-li2022].
audit.bottom_line: Accurate.

audit.claim: Top-fifth crucifer intake is linked to ~22% lower mortality; a feeding trial lowered IL-6 19%.
audit.biases: The 22% figure is from Shanghai cohorts, observational [adiet-zhang2011]; the feeding trial's other markers were inconsistent [adiet-navarro2014].
audit.newer_evidence: Umbrella review rates most crucifer associations weak or suggestive [adiet-li2022].
audit.bottom_line: The associations are observational; treat them as plausible, not proven.

audit.claim: 85 g/day watercress cut lymphocyte DNA damage 17% in 60 adults; PEITC modestly shifted carcinogen metabolism in smokers.
audit.biases: Small trials; single-centre.
audit.newer_evidence: No replication found [adiet-gill2007, adiet-yuan2016].
audit.bottom_line: Accurate and appropriately limited.

audit.claim: Moringa showed an acute glucose effect but a 2025 meta-analysis found no consistent cardiometabolic effect.
audit.biases: Small heterogeneous trials.
audit.newer_evidence: The 2025 meta-analysis remains the latest [adiet-crisan2025].
audit.bottom_line: Accurate.

audit.claim: Carotenoid foods are linked to less oxidative damage, but beta-carotene pills raised lung cancer and mortality in smokers.
audit.biases: The food associations are observational; the supplement result is the classic case where randomized trials overturned cohort-based expectations [adiet-omenn1996].
audit.newer_evidence: Cochrane confirms beta-carotene supplements increase mortality [adiet-bjelakovic2012].
audit.bottom_line: Accurate; a model antioxidant-paradox entry.

audit.claim: Plasma vitamin C saturates near 200 mg/day from food; high-dose pills show no mortality benefit.
audit.biases: None material; depletion-repletion pharmacokinetics are experimental [adiet-levine1996].
audit.newer_evidence: Cochrane supplement data unchanged [adiet-bjelakovic2012].
audit.bottom_line: Accurate.

audit.claim: 500 mg/day hesperidin or orange juice lowered diastolic BP in small crossover trials; meta-analysis shows modest effects.
audit.biases: Small, short, partly industry-linked trials.
audit.newer_evidence: The 2025 meta-analysis is current [adiet-heidari2025, adiet-morand2011].
audit.bottom_line: Accurate.

audit.claim: Lycopene is more bioavailable from cooked paste; tomato interventions lower LDL and IL-6; one lycopene trial missed its semen primary endpoint.
audit.biases: Short trials; the sperm trial was underpowered [adiet-williams2020].
audit.newer_evidence: No newer contrary synthesis found [adiet-cheng2017].
audit.bottom_line: Accurate.

audit.claim: Garlic supplements lower BP in hypertensives; oxidative-marker meta-analysis is weak.
audit.biases: Small heterogeneous trials with implausibly large effect sizes on oxidative markers [adiet-askari2021].
audit.newer_evidence: No newer contrary synthesis found [adiet-ried2016].
audit.bottom_line: Accurate.

audit.claim: Culinary turmeric produces only nanomolar curcumin conjugates in blood; no systemic antioxidant effect shown.
audit.biases: Population 'curry eater' associations are confounded.
audit.newer_evidence: Pharmacokinetic data remain decisive [adiet-mahale2018].
audit.bottom_line: Accurate.
